sounds.intro: Basque (Euskara) is spoken in the Basque Country. It is unrelated to any other language in the world. This is standard Basque (Batua). It is spelled quite regularly.
rows: y, like "yes" (in some regions a harsh h)
notes: Stress is light and falls usually on the second syllable of a word, but it varies by region. The say column shows approximate sounds.
The verb goes last. Basque uses cases (endings) instead of prepositions: etxe (house), etxean (in the house), etxera (to the house).

phrases.title: Formal and informal
phrases.note: Basque has formal "zu" (for strangers) and informal "hi" (very close friends and family, rarely used by learners). Use "zu" with everybody.

vocab.title: Common verbs
vocab.note: Dictionary form. "Izan" and "egon" are both "to be". "Ukan" is "to have".

grammar.title: Pronouns
text: Basque usually drops the subject pronoun, because the verb shows who is acting. "zu" is you (polite singular), "zuek" is you all.

grammar.title: Singular and plural
text: There is no "a" and no gender. "The" is the ending -a (singular) or -ak (plural): etxea (the house), etxeak (the houses). "A / one" is "bat" after the noun: etxe bat.

grammar.title: Izan and egon: to be
text: "Izan" is for who or what someone is: ikaslea naiz. "Egon" is for where and how: etxean nago.

grammar.title: Ukan: to have
text: "Ukan" gives the form "dut" (I have), "duzu" (you have), "du" (he/she has), "dugu" (we have), "dute" (they have). Hunger is expressed with "izan": gose naiz (I am hungry).

grammar.title: Verbs: present tense
text: Most Basque verbs have two parts: the main verb (jaten, hitz egiten) and a helper (dut, duzu, du...). The helper shows who does it. "Jaten dut" = I eat.

grammar.title: Joan: to go
text: "Joan" has its own forms: noa (I go), zoaz (you go), doa (he goes), goaz (we go), doaz (they go). "Hara" or "-ra" shows the place you go to.

grammar.title: Basic sentences
text: The verb goes at the end. Order: subject, object, verb. The subject of an action takes -k: Mariak liburua irakurtzen du.
ex: we live in a big house

grammar.title: Negation
text: Put "ez" before the verb helper: ez dut nahi. After a negative, a noun takes -rik: ez dut autorik (I have no car). Always compare with the positive form.
ex: I do not have a car
he does not work on Sundays

grammar.title: Asking questions
text: Add "al" before the verb helper for a yes-or-no question: ingelesez hitz egiten al duzu? In speech a rising voice is enough.

grammar.title: Possessives
text: Possessives come before the noun: nire etxea (my house), zure lagunak (your friends). Liking is expressed as "it pleases me": musika gustatzen zait.

grammar.title: Formal vs informal
text: "Zu" is the polite form for one person. "Hi" is the very familiar form for close friends. "Jauna" is sir, "andrea" is madam.

grammar.title: Past and future (simple)
text: Past: the helper changes (nuen, zuen). Future: add -ko / -go to the verb: joango naiz (I will go).

grammar.title: Commands
text: The command is a special verb form. Negative: "ez" + the command form, e.g. ez etorri. Add "mesedez" to be polite.

grammar.title: Can, must, want
text: ahal = can, behar = must, nahi = want. "Ezin dut" = I cannot. "Joan behar dut" = I must go. "Jan nahi dut" = I want to eat. The helper stays at the end.
ex: I do not want to eat

grammar.title: In, on, at
text: Basque uses endings: -n = in / at (etxean), -ra = to (etxera), -tik = from (etxetik). "Gainean" = on, "azpian" = under, "ondoan" = next to, "gertu" = near.
ex: the book is on the table
the cat is under the table
the shop is next to the bank
the park is near the station
the key is in the bag

grammar.title: Comparing things
text: Add -ago to the adjective for "more": handi, handiago (bigger). Add -en for "most": handien. "Baino" = than: hau hura baino handiagoa da.
